title: AI's Real Value Isn't Speed—It's Doing What We Never Dared Imagine
dek: Productivity metrics count code output and bugs, but miss the real shift: teams now solve harder problems they'd previously deemed impractical or impossible. That's precisely why Titus Winters argues AI's impact is wildly underestimated.
why: Direct account of Google's testing culture and how it orchestrated a 250-million-line refactor, plus concrete ideas for teaching CS in the AI era. Information-dense throughout.
who: Engineering leaders, infrastructure team leads, and anyone rethinking CS education for the age of AI.
skip: Skip the opening ~13 minutes (0:00–13:00) on childhood and hiring—low information density.

points.h: A production outage forced testing from virtue to non-negotiable rule.
points.body: Around 2006–07, Google Search was plagued by regressions. Releases slowed from monthly to quarterly. The system was monolithic—a Gmail change could break Search. Release engineers drew a hard line: no tests, no merge, regardless of VP rank or deadline urgency. After that line, fear stopped being tolerated as an engineering excuse. It had to be technical.

points.h: Twelve engineers rewrote a foundation serving 250 million lines without shutdown.
points.body: Google's internal C++ base was roughly 250 million lines, with nearly 10,000 engineers modifying it monthly. Titus led a 10–12 person team rebuilding core infrastructure—caches, containers, strings, command-line parsing—everything else depended on it. They described the work as replacing the Empire State Building's foundation while keeping it open to traffic, then discovering nuclear waste in the basement.

points.h: Compilers can rewrite code more reliably than humans at scale.
points.body: The team didn't manually edit each call site. Instead they parsed code into an Abstract Syntax Tree using Clang/LLVM, matched specific call patterns precisely, then auto-generated edits—a MapReduce-style refactor. Even formatting became blocking; Titus pushed Clang-format, now widely used. The pattern: ship old and new APIs together, migrate directory by directory, delete old code only after verifying no callers remain. This cycle repeated hundreds of times.

points.h: AI should write the rules once, not rewrite endlessly.
points.body: For large-scale refactors, Titus advises against repeated AI inference. Better: have AI generate a declarative rewrite config (like OpenRewrite)—fix the pattern and transformation once, then run it deterministically across millions of lines. Cheaper, more accurate, more auditable. Kelsey Hightower's principle: if your entire architecture needs continuous inference, a cheaper and more reliable alternative probably exists.

points.h: A 15-question survey outpredicts any engineering metric we have.
points.body: A brief psychological safety survey predicts roughly 30% of variance in whether a team achieves its goals—stronger than any other signal Titus has encountered. His response: if you believe software engineering excludes emotion, find a stronger predictor. You won't. This isn't a one-time game; it's repeated play. Teams that admit when they're stuck get stronger.

points.h: Current metrics can't measure the problems AI made worth solving.
points.body: Titus sorts technical impact into four categories: product wins, compute efficiency, engineering velocity, and game-changing shifts. Writing a JPEG parser in a few weeks would sound absurd three years ago, but metrics only count throughput, not that you're now building "gold-plated widgets" you never imagined before. Real example: engineers rewrote a third-party component using AI against an existing test suite—work that normally took 5–10 people years and 5–15% annual revenue in licensing fees. The vendor paid to keep it closed. Planned layoffs were canceled.

points.h: CS curricula were frozen in time around the year 2000.
points.body: Titus was the only working engineer on the ACM/IEEE undergraduate curriculum committee. The system was built for nineties-style databases and OSes, then just packed with more topics and diluted. Even before AI arrived, he argued it should burn and restart: less hand-coded linked lists, more systems thinking, specs, and test-driven validation.

points.h: Evaluate what the student prompted, not what AI wrote.
points.body: Students can now AI-complete most assignments. Titus doesn't block it; he adapts. Assume they're using AI; grade the process instead—what prompts did you write, what tests did you write to verify the output? That principle applies beyond CS; nobody needs another ‘Catcher in the Rye’ essay. What matters is whether the student struggled, thought hard, and learned.
